blocks.text: The vineyard song gives the chapter’s central accusation a concrete form: God expected justice and righteousness from Israel and Judah, but the chapter instead names oppression, corrupt judgment, exploitation, and disregard for God’s work. The later woes are therefore not separate complaints; they develop what the vineyard’s bad fruit represents. God’s holiness is joined here to justice and righteousness, so public wrongdoing cannot be treated as compatible with belonging to him.

The Great Isaiah Scroll preserves nearly the whole sixty-six-chapter book of Isaiah and is broadly aligned with the Masoretic tradition, though it contains many spelling and substantive differences. Other Isaiah manuscripts and interpretive texts from Qumran also show that Isaiah was actively copied and interpreted. The significance of particular differences remains disputed.

sections.title: A note on Isaiah’s textual transmission
